statements.quote: so we can flip to UHC, CVS, Carelon, or another major player in 2 to 4 years. That's the whole game.
statements.context: Chapter six of the author's Wizard of Oz health-tech parody. The fictional Private Equity Investor explains the PE playbook to the Founder of the fictional startup inFlames: invest after traction, then flip the company to UnitedHealthcare, CVS, Carelon or another major player within 2 to 4 years.
statements.note: Satirical fiction; spoken by a fictional PE investor about a fictional startup. Underlying claim is a generic description of the PE exit playbook, not a dated call.

statements.quote: is moving to release more of these “complete response letters.” (CRL)
statements.context: Opening of a post on the FDA's complete response letter for the Lykos/MAPS MDMA-assisted therapy application. The author says the FDA, as part of a push toward transparency, is moving to release more CRLs publicly.
statements.note: Describes an in-progress agency trend; implies more CRL releases to come.

statements.quote: To expect your drug-therapy Frankenstein to get approved is quixotic at best.
statements.context: After quoting the CRL's finding that MAPP2 adverse-event definitions did not match what the FDA asked for, the author says that expecting approval of the MDMA plus MAPS-branded therapy combination is quixotic.
statements.note: Negative call on approval prospects for the MDMA-AT drug-plus-branded-therapy submission.

statements.quote: MAPS promises to continue “training therapists” in its dubious approach.
statements.context: The author reports that MAPS (the non-profit) has promised to keep training therapists in its MDMA-assisted therapy approach despite the CRL; he then cites the FDA's recommendation to use evidence-based standard-of-care psychotherapy instead.
statements.note: Third-party stated intent relayed by the author; he disparages the approach but does not dispute that MAPS will continue.

statements.quote: The MAPS mission of getting a therapy cult over the line as an FDA-approved therapeutic is dead .
statements.context: After quoting the CRL's recommendation to use evidence-based standard-of-care psychotherapy instead of the MAPS-developed psychotherapy in future studies, the author declares the MAPS mission of FDA approval for its branded therapy dead.
statements.note: Negative call: MAPS-branded psychotherapy will not become an FDA-approved therapeutic. Verbatim text has a space before the final period.

statements.quote: any future psychedelic-assisted therapy trials intended for approval from FDA won’t include kooky inner healing intelligen ce or recreating psychotherapy from scratch.
statements.context: Summary conclusion after the CRL advised a factorial design with a no-psychotherapy arm and evidence-based standard-of-care psychotherapy: the author predicts that future FDA-approval psychedelic trials will not use MAPS-style 'inner healing intelligence' or newly invented psychotherapies.
statements.note: Verbatim text splits 'intelligence' as 'intelligen ce'.

statements.quote: We're going to keep up that cadence this year.
statements.context: Programming notes at the end of a parenting essay. RAMHT (the author's rapid acting mental health treatment events) held live events in San Francisco in July (concurrent with a JPM health conference) and in May (concurrent with the American Psychiatric Association meeting); the author says they will keep that cadence this year.
statements.note: Own-organization event plan. Coder may mark CONTROL.

statements.quote: we're going to have an AI-focused event for JPM Health.
statements.context: Same programming note: the one change to the RAMHT event cadence is an AI-focused event timed with the JPM health conference; the author invites sponsors to reach out.
statements.note: Own-organization event plan. Coder may mark CONTROL.

statements.quote: a medical device company that is bringing an at-home depression treatment device through the FDA right now.
statements.context: Programming note: the author says his second job is at Neurolief, which is taking an at-home depression treatment device (eCOT-AS) through the FDA; he mentions the MOOD study just published in Brain Stimulation.
statements.note: Describes an ongoing FDA submission for the author's own company; implies an expected FDA decision. Coder may mark CONTROL.

statements.quote: soon, eCOT-AS by Neurolief
statements.context: Radial promotional footer listing treatments offered: Spravato, Nightware, eTNS, PRISM Neurofeedback, 'soon, eCOT-AS by Neurolief', TMS, Accelerated TMS and fMRI-guided SAINT TMS. Implies Radial will soon offer Neurolief's eCOT-AS device.
statements.note: Boilerplate footer repeated across posts (also in depression-can-be-over-in-6-half). Own organizations; coder may mark CONTROL.

statements.quote: Our children, I fear, will judge us harshly for the choices we’ve made.
statements.context: Essay on US gun deaths after Charlie Kirk's killing. The author argues children notice mass shootings and will form opinions; he fears future harsh judgment from children for the choice to privilege gun access over child safety.
statements.note: Social/rhetorical forecast; preceded by 'My children, your children, Mr. Kirk's children, will all have an opinion.'

statements.quote: why I think this drug, and others like it, might actually be best understood as a turning point for Medicaid plans.
statements.context: Thesis of a post on MindMed's phase 2b JAMA paper on MM-120 (oral LSD) for GAD: the author thinks single-dose psychedelics like MM-120 may become a turning point for Medicaid plans because rapid remission could save money within short enrollment spans.
statements.note: Author discloses about 500 MindMed shares and a past PI role on MindMed trials.

statements.quote: MM-120, if approved, is a single-dose treatment with durability that could quickly realize its benefits in individuals on Medicaid, potentially accomplishing the almost impossible task of saving money in a Medicaid health plan.
statements.context: Crux of the argument: conditional on FDA approval, MM-120's single-dose fast-acting profile could save money for Medicaid plans, which the author calls almost impossible normally because average Medicaid enrollment is measured in months.
statements.note: Conditional on approval; compound (approval plus plan savings).

statements.quote: If MM120 works in a single day and single dose, and people who don't have anxiety get back to work, that alone could reduce the number of Medicaid beneficiaries out of work.
statements.context: Conditional claim that fast GAD remission from MM120 could reduce the number of Medicaid beneficiaries who are out of work, which the author says is good for state budgets.
statements.note: Conditional mechanism claim.

statements.quote: since MM120 works so quickly, the savings might be realized in the timeframe in which the individual is on the plan.
statements.context: Even for beneficiaries who stay on Medicaid but change plans, the author says a Medicaid plan might realize MM120-driven savings within the enrollee's time on the plan (average 11.6 months over a 12-month span).
statements.note: Hedged mechanism claim tied to short Medicaid enrollment spans.

statements.quote: This story will get even stronger if MM120 gets a major depressive disorder indication.
statements.context: The author notes MindMed also runs phase III trials for MDD; if MM120 gets an MDD indication, the Medicaid savings case becomes stronger.
statements.note: Conditional on a future MDD indication.

statements.quote: We might have a very rare combination of excellent outcomes, limited risks, and the ability to drive savings with one treatment if the data from the phase 2b trial is replicated in subsequent studies and into the real world.
statements.context: Closing hedge: the favorable outcome, risk and savings profile of MM-120 holds if the phase 2b results replicate in phase III and in real-world use.
statements.note: Conditional on replication of phase 2b data.

statements.quote: More treatments exist, and are coming too. One addresses anhedonia and doesn’t hurt at all—brand name PRISM-MDD . Another, ProLivRx, can be done entirely at home .
statements.context: After describing the FDA clearance (granted the day of the post) of the Brainsway accelerated deep TMS protocol, the author says more depression treatments are coming: PRISM-MDD (anhedonia, painless), ProLivRx (fully at home), and psychedelics.
statements.note: Compound: several upcoming treatments named; 'Let's not forget psychedelics!' follows. Verbatim text has spaces before periods.

statements.quote: soon, eCOT-AS by Neurolief
statements.context: Radial promotional footer listing treatments offered: Spravato, Nightware, eTNS, PRISM Neurofeedback, 'soon, eCOT-AS by Neurolief', TMS, Accelerated TMS and fMRI-guided SAINT TMS. Implies Radial will soon offer Neurolief's eCOT-AS device.
statements.note: Boilerplate footer repeated from dont-tell-kids-it-will-be-okay. Own organizations; coder may mark CONTROL.

statements.quote: It's also probably a decision to keep all of us safer, to keep those interested in the dreadful combination of murder and suicide away from guns, and maybe even reduce mass shootings.
statements.context: Discussing population-level means restriction (limiting access to guns), the author says that beyond protecting undetected high-risk individuals, it is probably a decision that keeps everyone safer and may reduce mass shootings.
statements.note: Hedged policy-effect claim; gun policy is outside the listed areas, so 'other'.

statements.quote: I stand firm that the data suggest that mass shootings only happen with guns, and that restricting access to guns would reduce mass shootings, because obviously.
statements.context: After conceding that individual-level evidence that firearm restriction reduces suicide is weak, the author holds firm that restricting access to guns would reduce mass shootings.
statements.note: Conditional policy-effect claim (if gun access is restricted, mass shootings fall).

statements.quote: I suspect that accelerated transcranial magnetic stimulation will also be effective, and we have some data to suggest that is the case.
statements.context: Closing of the suicide-prevention essay: after noting that ketamine is rapidly effective at reducing suicidality in treatment-seeking people, the author predicts accelerated TMS will also be effective for reducing suicidality.
statements.note: The author's clinic (Radial) offers accelerated TMS and he is an accelerated TMS researcher; coder may consider CONTROL.

statements.quote: Police believe they may still find victims in the burned-out building.
statements.context: The author quotes a news report on the Michigan church attack (vehicle rammed through the front, shooting, fire): police believe more victims may be found in the burned building.
statements.note: Quoted news report (police expectation), not the author's claim; logged for recall.

statements.quote: No one's gonna remember who you are either. There are too many of these events.
statements.context: Addressing potential future gunmen, arsonists and mass murderers, the author asserts they will not be remembered because such events are too frequent; he ties this to research on media contagion of mass shootings and his refusal to name the shooter.
statements.note: Rhetorical address to would-be shooters; reinforced by 'no one will remember you, or the horrible things you thought about doing.'
